body.statement: For every optimal support cell and every replacement atom in the same arm, \(\phi_{at}\ge\phi_{as}+g(z_{at}-z_{as})\) for each \(g\in G_{as}\).  Hence, if \(z_{as}<z_{at}\), every \(g\in G_{as}\) and \(h\in G_{at}\) obey \(g\le[\phi_{at}-\phi_{as}]/[z_{at}-z_{as}]\le h\).  The intervals \(I_{as}\) are strictly ordered and disjoint within each arm, with \(I_{1s},I_{2s}\subset[-1/2,5/4]\) and \(I_{3s}\subset[-3/2,0]\).  If \(I_{as}\) and \(I_{at}\) lie in one interval of length \(H\), then \(|z_{at}-z_{as}|\le H\) and \(0\le\phi_{at}-\phi_{as}-g(z_{at}-z_{as})\le H^2\), including ties and grid-boundary contacts under the singleton convention.
body.justification: The exact arm-specific slope roots are the cost-specific mechanism that makes the multiscale repair quadratic and reduces the universal constant.
body.gap: Gao, Ge, and Qian (2025, Lemma on finite-support optimal couplings) use coordinate exchanges to bound support sums; they do not derive ordered scalar dual intervals or an integer-repair modulus.
body.consumer: The ranges of lengths seven-fourths, seven-fourths, and three-halves determine the summable per-scale charge in the deterministic rounding algorithm.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an arm \(a\), an atom \(s\in S_a\), a cell \(e\in E\) with \(e_a=s\), and put
\[
 w=\sum_{b\ne a}z_{be_b},\qquad g=-2w.
\]
By the definition of \(G_{as}\), every member of \(G_{as}\) arises in this way from some such support cell.  Dual feasibility and tightness on \(E\), as recorded in the definition of \(u_{as}\), give
\[
 u_{as}+\sum_{b\ne a}u_{be_b}=(z_{as}+w)^2
\]
and, after replacing only coordinate \(a\) by an arbitrary \(t\in S_a\),
\[
 u_{at}+\sum_{b\ne a}u_{be_b}\le (z_{at}+w)^2.
\]
Subtracting the first display from the second and using \(\phi_{ar}=z_{ar}^2-u_{ar}\) yields
\[
 \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}
 \ge -2w(z_{at}-z_{as})
 =g(z_{at}-z_{as}). \tag{1}
\]
This proves the first assertion for every \(g\in G_{as}\).  Each distinct marginal atom has positive multiplicity; because \(q^\star\) has that marginal, the atom is incident to a cell of its positive support \(E\).  Thus every \(G_{as}\) is nonempty.

Suppose \(z_{as}<z_{at}\) and set \(d=z_{at}-z_{as}>0\).  Apply (1) first from \(s\) to \(t\), and then from \(t\) to \(s\).  For every \(g\in G_{as}\) and \(h\in G_{at}\), this gives
\[
 gd\le \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}\le hd,
 \qquad
 g\le \frac{\phi_{at}-\phi_{as}}{z_{at}-z_{as}}\le h. \tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(\max G_{as}\le\min G_{at}\), and therefore
\[
 z_{as}+\max G_{as}<z_{at}+\min G_{at}. \tag{3}
\]
Thus the closed intervals \(I_{as}\) are strictly ordered by \(z_{as}\) and are pairwise disjoint within each arm.  The fixed contrast and the support \([0,1]\) give
\[
 z_1,z_2\in[0,1/4],\qquad z_3\in[-1/2,0].
\]
For \(a=1\) or \(a=2\), the sum of the other two coordinates belongs to \([-1/2,1/4]\), whereas for \(a=3\) it belongs to \([0,1/2]\).  Consequently
\[
 G_{1s},G_{2s}\subset[-1/2,1],\qquad G_{3s}\subset[-1,0],
\]
and hence
\[
 I_{1s},I_{2s}\subset[-1/2,5/4],\qquad
 I_{3s}\subset[-3/2,0]. \tag{4}
\]

Finally, suppose that \(I_{as}\) and \(I_{at}\) are contained in a common interval \(J\) of length \(H\).  If \(s=t\), both claimed quantities vanish.  If \(z_{as}<z_{at}\), choose \(g\in G_{as}\) and \(h\in G_{at}\).  By (2), \(h-g\ge0\), while the two points \(z_{as}+g,z_{at}+h\in J\) obey
\[
 (z_{at}-z_{as})+(h-g)
 =(z_{at}+h)-(z_{as}+g)\le H. \tag{5}
\]
Both nonnegative summands in (5) are at most \(H\).  If \(m=[\phi_{at}-\phi_{as}]/[z_{at}-z_{as}]\), then (2) gives \(g\le m\le h\), and therefore
\[
 |z_{at}-z_{as}|\le H,\quad
 0\le \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}-g(z_{at}-z_{as})
 =(m-g)(z_{at}-z_{as})
 \le H^2. \tag{6}
\]
If \(z_{at}<z_{as}\), reverse the order.  Then, for \(h\in G_{at}\), the corresponding secant slope satisfies \(h\le m\le g\), and the remainder is \((g-m)(z_{as}-z_{at})\); the analogue of (5) again bounds both factors by \(H\).  Aggregating repeated observations leaves one atom and positive multiplicity, so it does not alter the argument.  A contact with a grid boundary changes only whether the algorithm declares an interval singleton; (1)--(6) are closed inequalities and remain valid.  This proves the lemma.
